posts.quote: REMEMBER WHEN WE BUILT BONFIRES LIKE THIS
posts.caption: It started the week before, with every kid on the block dragging home whatever wood he could find. Pallets, fence boards, an old door, a broken chair somebody's dad finally said we could have. By Saturday the pile stood taller than the garage, and every one of us had to climb it at least once for the picture. Nobody asked a grownup if it was a good idea, and the grownups mostly pretended not to see. When it finally came down in a roar of orange and sparks, the whole street stood in a circle with red faces and sticky hands. You could feel it on your cheeks until you fell asleep.
posts.first: We built ours in the empty lot behind the Hendersons' and I hauled boards for six days straight. My father walked over on Saturday, looked it up and down, and said he'd seen worse. That was about the nicest thing he ever said to me.

posts.character: Cars and driving culture (the family motel)
posts.quote: THE MOTEL HAD A NEON SIGN, A SWIMMING POOL, AND ONE ROOM FOR ALL FIVE OF US.
posts.caption: After eleven hours in the back seat, that neon sign was the most beautiful thing in the state. Dad went into the office alone and came back swinging a key on a big plastic tag. Five of us piled into one room with two beds and a fan in the window, and nobody complained because there was a pool. Mom hung wet swimsuits over every chair while Dad studied the map by the bedside lamp. We fell asleep to the hum of the ice machine and the trucks on the highway, certain we had never been so far from home.
posts.first: We stayed in a place just like that on the way to see my grandparents in Ohio. I got the spot on the floor between the beds and thought it was the best seat in the house. My father tipped the man at the desk a quarter and acted like he had just bought the place.

posts.quote: What smell takes you straight back to your grandmother's kitchen, no matter where you are?
posts.first: Mine is yeast rolls rising under a dish towel, with a little cinnamon from the pie. I only have to think of it and I'm standing on her linoleum again. I'd give a lot to smell it for real once more.

posts.quote: THERE WAS ALWAYS ENOUGH FOOD, A LITTLE CHAOS, AND A MOM WHO MADE EVERYONE FEEL LIKE THEY BELONGED.
posts.caption: Nobody ever called ahead. A friend would show up at suppertime and Mom would just pull out another chair and another plate. The sandwiches came off the counter faster than she could make them, and there was always a jar of something open next to the bread. The refrigerator door was covered with school photos, report cards, and drawings, and the phone on the wall had a cord stretched to the next room. It was loud, it was crowded, and somebody always had milk on their sleeve. And somehow every kid who walked through that door left feeling like they'd been expected.
posts.first: There was always one extra kid at our table, and half the time I didn't know whose he was. My mother would put a plate in front of him and ask him how his mother was. I think that kitchen raised more children than my parents ever counted.

posts.quote: THE LUNCH LADY / A HAIRNET, A LADLE, AND A LOOK THAT MADE YOU FINISH YOUR PEAS
posts.caption: Every school had one, and she ran that cafeteria like a ship. Hairnet tight, ladle ready, she could tell from the end of the line which kid was about to ask for seconds and which one was about to hide his peas. Nobody ever saw her smile, but she somehow knew your name and whether you had your milk money. The rectangular pizza came on Fridays and the line for it started before the bell. She worked harder than anyone in the building, and most of us never thought to say thank you.
posts.first: Ours was a woman named Mrs. Pruitt who once slipped me an extra roll when she saw I had forgotten my lunch. She never mentioned it and neither did I. I think about that roll every time I hear a school bell.

posts.quote: THOSE TWO COULDN'T AGREE ON A DAMN THING. BUT NEITHER ONE WAS GOING TO LET THE OTHER FREEZE.
posts.caption: They had argued about politics, baseball, and the right way to stack wood for forty years. Every fall the one with the pickup showed up in the other's yard without a word. The wood came off the tailgate one split log at a time and went up the stack in neat rows. Neither of them said thank you, and neither of them needed to hear it. They might not speak again until the first snow, when the second one would turn up with a thermos of coffee. That was how men of that age said what they couldn't put into words.
posts.first: My granddad and his neighbor Earl never agreed on anything, and they were the best of friends. Earl split wood for my grandfather the winter his back went out and wouldn't take a nickel. Granddad paid him back in tomatoes, and they both pretended that was a fair trade.

posts.quote: Finish this sentence: In our house, the one rule nobody ever dared to break was...
posts.first: In ours it was that nobody touched the food until Dad had said grace and sat down. I once reached for a roll too early and got a look that lasted the whole prayer. I have never forgotten it.

posts.quote: HOW MANY OF YOU REMEMBER TAKING EMPTY SODA BOTTLES BACK TO THE STORE FOR MONEY?
posts.caption: A wooden crate of empty bottles by the back door was a savings account in plain sight. You hauled it down to the corner store between two kids, because one alone couldn't carry it without a stop every ten steps. The man behind the counter counted them out loud and slid you a few coins for every one. Two cents a bottle felt like a fortune on a hot afternoon. By the time you walked out, the money was already spent in your head on a candy bar and a cold drink. And sometimes you ended up buying a bottle of the same soda you had just turned in.
posts.first: My cousin and I once collected bottles from every ditch in our neighborhood and made almost two dollars. We spent the whole thing at the corner store in about four minutes. I can still taste that grape soda.

posts.quote: THE MAILMAN KNEW EVERY DOG ON THE ROUTE BY NAME, AND EVERY DOG KNEW HIM.
posts.caption: He walked the same route every day in rain, sleet, and the occasional blizzard, with a heavy leather bag cutting into one shoulder. Every dog on the street was waiting at its gate when he turned the corner. He carried a pocketful of biscuits and handed them out like a man giving communion. He knew who was expecting a letter from the Army and who dreaded the one from the bank. Somebody always had a glass of iced tea waiting on the porch rail, and he drank it standing up, mailbag and all.
posts.first: Our mailman was a man named Walt who walked our street for thirty-one years. My mother saved him the first tomato from the garden every summer. When he retired the whole block came out on the sidewalk and he pretended not to notice.

posts.character: Humor about today vs. then (the VCR)
posts.quote: REMEMBER THE DAY YOUR FAMILY BROUGHT HOME A VCR AND SUDDENLY YOU COULD WATCH WHATEVER YOU WANTED WHENEVER YOU WANTED? THAT WAS BRAND NEW.
posts.caption: Dad spent the entire evening on his knees in front of the television with a booklet and a handful of cables. Mom stood behind him with her arms crossed, saying nothing, which was somehow worse than advice. The kids sat on the couch holding their breath while the screen turned to static. Nobody breathed again until a picture finally flickered on. For the first time in history, you could stop a program and finish it after supper. Dad leaned back on his heels like he had just landed a plane.
posts.first: Our first one was the size of a suitcase, and Dad made us promise to rewind everything before we pushed the button. The tape of my birthday party got recorded over by a ball game within a month. He swore it wasn't his fault.
